newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Tycoon Tung declared Hong Kong handover leader.
newsitem.headline: Tycoon Tung declared Hong Kong handover leader.

text.p: Shipping magnate Tung Chee-hwa swept effortlessly to a historic victory on Wednesday in the poll to select Hong Kong's leader-in-waiting to take over when the British colony reverts to Chinese rule next year.

Hong Kong's new elite, a 400-strong Selection Committee carefully assembled by Beijing, overwhelmingly voted for the 59-year-old businessman, whose family maritime empire was bailed out by China a decade ago.
Tung becomes chief executive-designate, destined to step into Governor Chris Patten's shoes when the British withdraw from their last Asian outpost at midnight on June 30, 1997.

When July 1 dawns, the red flag of China will flutter over the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region of China, a quasi-autonomous territory that China has promised can maintain its capitalist freedoms intact for 50 years.

"I am announcing that Tung Chee-hwa is elected as the first Hong Kong Special Adminstrative Region chief executive," declared China'a Foreign Minister Qian Qichen, who made only his second visit to Hong Kong to chair the ballot.
Tung, 59, collected 320 votes. His nearest rival, former chief justice Yang Ti Liang, received 42. The third contender, businessman Peter Woo polled 36, and two votes were spoiled.
"We would like to congratulate Mr Tung," Qian told committee members seated in long lines in a style redolent of ceremonies in Beijing's Great Hall of the People.
The outcome was considered a foregone conclusion in Hong Kong, where the media put the finishing touches to celebratory editions before voting even started.

China hailed the process as the birth of genuine democracy in the tiny but wealthy community of six million people, to the fury of Hong Kong's democracy lobby, which denounced the ballot as a travesty and boycotted the process.
Activists screaming "oppose the phoney election" scuffled with riot police outside the hall where the vote took place.

One of Hong Kong's best-known pro-democracy politicians, Emily Lau, was dragged away kicking and screaming by police after lying down in the road in protest against China's methods of choosing the future leader.
Lau has scheduled a no-confidence debate on the future leadership in the Legislative Council later in the day. Protesters camped overnight outside the conference centre.

Tung's public comments espousing "consensus" rather than confrontation with China, and collective duties over individual rights, have worried pro-democracy activists. They fret about China-style repression creeping into Hong Kong after the handover.
"The people of Hong Kong cannot trust him to protect our rights...I cannot see how he is in a position to say no to Beijing on any important issue," said legislator Martin Lee ahead of the ballot.
Polls had earlier indicated Tung was the favoured candidate of Hong Kong's influential business community.
Hong Kong's stock market, which has enjoyed a recent boom, climbed 75.12 points to 13,417.58 during active morning trade, gains brokers said were inspired in part by Tung's success.
"With Tung Chee-hwa in the leadership position, Hong Kong will have the most pro-business government in recent history," said Janet Gillis, sales director at OCBC Securities.
